fields.h1: The Bruised Reed: Richard Sibbes for the Discouraged
fields.meta_title: The Bruised Reed Explained — Richard Sibbes’s Comfort for the Discouraged
fields.description: A guide to Richard Sibbes’s The Bruised Reed: the promise from Isaiah behind it, how Christ deals with the weak and the discouraged, the signs of true grace in a smoking wick, and how to read this gentlest of the Puritans.
fields.body_html:
The Bruised Reed is a book about how Jesus treats people who are weak, discouraged, and barely holding on. It was written by Richard Sibbes, a much-loved English preacher of the early 1600s, and it takes its title and its whole theme from a single verse in Isaiah: the bruised reed he will not break, and the smoking flax he will not quench. Where much Puritan writing is stern, this one is tender, and it has comforted anxious Christians for four hundred years. It was the book that helped turn Richard Baxter toward Christ, and it has quietly kept many others from giving up.

This guide explains the promise behind the book, how Sibbes says Christ deals with the bruised and the smoking, the signs of real grace in a person who feels they have almost none, and how to read it. The full text is free in the Ochorus library.

The promise behind the book

The verse is Isaiah 42:3, quoted about Jesus in Matthew 12:20: “A bruised reed shall he not break, and smoking flax shall he not quench.” Sibbes takes it apart gently. A reed is a weak thing to begin with, and a bruised reed is weaker still — bent, crushed, fit only to be thrown away. Smoking flax is the wick of a lamp that has almost gone out: no flame, just a red thread and a little smoke, the kind of thing anyone would pinch out. These, Sibbes says, are the people Christ came for. Not the strong and the flourishing, but the crushed and the nearly extinguished. Matthew 12:20 adds the promise that he will keep at it “till he send forth judgment unto victory” — he does not merely spare the weak, he brings them through to triumph.

Sibbes’s whole book is an unfolding of that mercy. His most quoted sentence sums it up:

There is more mercy in Christ than sin in us.

Richard Sibbes, The Bruised Reed

The bruising comes first

Sibbes begins somewhere surprising: he says that being bruised is necessary. Before a person will come to Christ, they usually have to be brought low enough to want him — to feel their sin, their weakness, their need. This is not cruelty; it is the ploughing before the sowing. The proud and the self-satisfied never come. It is the bruised who come. Jesus said he came to bind up the brokenhearted, Isaiah 61:1, and Psalm 51:17 says that a broken and contrite heart God will not despise. So Sibbes tells the discouraged reader that the very bruising they resent may be the thing bringing them home, and that it is, in his blunt phrase, “better to go bruised to heaven than sound to hell.”

But — and here is the tenderness — the bruising is never meant to destroy. Christ bruises only to heal. Sibbes describes him as a physician who specialises in exactly these cases:

He is a physician good at all diseases, especially at the binding up of a broken heart.

Richard Sibbes, The Bruised Reed

How Christ treats the weak

The heart of the book is a portrait of Christ’s gentleness with beginners and stragglers. Sibbes insists on several things that anxious believers constantly forget.

Grace is small at first, and Christ does not despise small beginnings. A new or struggling faith is like the smoking wick — more smoke than flame — and Christ, far from snuffing it, cups his hand around it and blows it into fire. Zechariah 4:10 asks who has despised the day of small things; Sibbes answers that Christ never does.

Grace is always mixed with corruption in this life. The believer is never pure gold yet; there is always dross mingled in. Sibbes will not let a Christian conclude they have no grace just because they still have sin. The wick smokes precisely because there is still fire in it. Romans 7:21–25 is the same experience — the good I would I do not — and Paul was no castaway.

Christ will not quench what he has kindled. This is the book’s central comfort. The Christ who began the little flame is committed to it, and will not let it go out. Philippians 1:6 is the promise Sibbes leans on constantly: he who began a good work will complete it.

Out of this Sibbes draws a pastoral rule for everyone else. If Christ is this gentle with the weak, then ministers, leaders, and ordinary Christians must be gentle too. He rebukes harsh, censorious believers who break bruised reeds that Christ would have spared. A church, he says, should be a place where the smoking flax is protected, not pinched out. Galatians 6:1 tells the spiritual to restore a fallen brother in meekness, and Sibbes makes that a duty for all.

Answering the discouraged

Much of the second half is Sibbes patiently removing the objections that discouraged people raise against themselves. But my grace is so weak. Weak grace is still grace, and Christ nurses it. But I am full of corruption. So was Paul; the flax smokes. But I keep failing. Christ’s work in you is not finished, and he does not abandon unfinished work. But maybe my desires are not real. Sibbes answers that a true desire for grace is itself grace — the very longing to love God is planted by God, as Matthew 5:6 blesses those who hunger and thirst after righteousness, promising they shall be filled.

He also warns against a particular enemy: listening to Satan’s portrait of Christ instead of Christ’s own. The accuser paints Jesus as reluctant, severe, easily put off — and a discouraged soul believes it. Sibbes tells the reader flatly not to believe Satan when he misrepresents Christ. Look instead at the Christ of the Gospels, who broke no bruised reed he ever met. Revelation 12:10 names Satan the accuser of the brethren; his accusations are not the verdict.

The gentleness is not weakness

It would be easy to misread Sibbes as merely soft, a comfort for people who never intend to change. He is not. The same Christ who will not break the bruised reed will, the verse promises, bring forth judgment unto victory — and Sibbes devotes the later chapters to that victory. The gentleness has a direction: Christ nurses the weak flame not to leave it smoking forever but to fan it into a blaze. His government in the soul is real; he subdues sin, strengthens grace, and carries the trembling believer through to triumph. Sibbes holds the two together perfectly: infinitely tender toward weakness, and utterly committed to overcoming it. The comfort is not that Christ leaves you as you are, but that he will not discard you while he changes you.

This is why the book has steadied so many. It refuses both of the lies a discouraged Christian is tempted to believe — that God is disgusted with their weakness and about to give up on them, and that their weakness therefore does not matter. Neither is true. The weakness matters, and it is being dealt with, gently, by a Saviour who finishes what he starts. 1 Thessalonians 5:24 is Sibbes’s confidence: faithful is he that calleth you, who also will do it.

Who Sibbes was

Richard Sibbes (1577–1635) was one of the best-loved preachers of his generation in England, known to his hearers as “the sweet dropper” for the gentleness of his preaching. He served as a lecturer at Gray’s Inn in London and as master of Katharine Hall in Cambridge, and he shaped a whole line of Puritan pastoral writers who followed him. He never married, gave much of what he had away, and preached a warm, Christ-centred, comforting divinity in an age that could tend toward severity. The Bruised Reed is the distilled essence of that ministry, and its long afterlife — it was still steering people like Richard Baxter to Christ within Sibbes’s own century, and steadying readers four hundred years later — is the best testimony to it.

How to read it today

Read it when you are low, not only when you are studying. This is a book for the discouraged, and it does its best work when you are one. Keep it for the days when faith feels like a smoking wick.

Do not rush past the bruising. Sibbes’s claim that bruising precedes comfort is easy to resent and important to receive. Let it reframe a hard season rather than skip it.

Read it slowly and devotionally. The seventeenth-century English rewards a gentle pace. Read a chapter as you might read a psalm, and let the comfort settle.

Read The God of All Comfort next. Hannah Whitall Smith’s book is Sibbes’s theme in a later voice — that God’s heart toward the weak is kindness — and the two reinforce each other across three centuries.

Then read a sermon like Sweet Comfort for Feeble Saints. Spurgeon, who loved the Puritans, preached the same gospel of gentleness to the weak, and hearing it from the pulpit completes what Sibbes teaches on the page.

Sibbes leaves the reader with one settled thing to hold: that the Christ who deals with them is gentler than they dare to believe, and more committed to them than their failures can undo. Isaiah 40:11 is his portrait of the Saviour — he shall gather the lambs with his arm, and gently lead those that are with young. The Bruised Reed is four hundred pages, in effect, of that one verse, pressed tenderly against a discouraged heart until it believes it.
